rv.q: Here again, with the original cast intact, is laughter, erupting continuously throughout Mark Gatiss’s impeccable production.
Social awkwardness is a staple of British comedy and there is much about The Unfriend that is very amusing, although some set pieces feel rather over-engineered.
None of the teasing or nudging lands much of a point, and edginess quickly evaporates – though there is an impressive performance from Gabriel Howell as a teenager who moves from slump to sunshine.
Strong performances energise this West End transfer of Steven Moffat’s light, likeable comedy
‘The Unfriend’ is unexciting, unadventurous and too often unfunny.
Instead, the ruthlessly unfunny scenario grinds on in Mark Gatiss’s production, pummelling ideas that weren’t amusing to start with into utter oblivion by over-extending them.
The Unfriend keeps you mirthfully on edge up to the final curtain.
The dialogue is admirably witty and inventive, and there are passages that would not disgrace Noël Coward.
The Unfriend is more multifaceted than it may first seem, as much as it is a comedy of manners it is also a comedy of menace.
I'd have preferred a more invigorating brew, but The Unfriend proves a genial escape from the winter blues.

Overall, there’s nothing wrong with the extended sitcom episode vibe that this production brings, but given this a 1 hour 40 minutes play with steep West End prices at the premium end, the question is whether it’s really worth it and if you’ll remember it the next day.
The Unfriend is a pleasantly funny show that loses its way somewhat as time goes on.
The Unfriend is national comedy gold packed with slapstick, social disasters and a toxically polite couple who can’t bring themselves to cause a fuss.
With its audience roaring from beginning to end, there’s hardly any doubt that this show is, undoubtedly, one of the strongest offers of the start of the year...

cn.t: Moffat and Gatiss's stage debut divides critics. While many praise its sharp wit and belly laughs, detractors dismiss it as lazy writing coasting on TV credentials. Barber's ferocious performance as the serial killer houseguest earns raves across the board.
